facts.text: New Egypt began as Timmon's Mill in the early 1700s, a mill town that grew around a water-powered gristmill on Oakford Lake.
In 1845 the settlement was renamed New Egypt to avoid confusion with another town called Egypt, a nod to biblical imagery of “going to Egypt for corn.”.
The Pemberton & Hightstown Railroad, completed in 1868, ran through New Egypt, turning the village into a brief resort spot in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
A former farmhouse on Evergreen Road now houses the New Egypt Historical Society Museum, preserving artifacts that trace the town’s agricultural roots.
Henry Charlton Beck noted Timmon's Mill as the approximate geographic center of New Jersey in his 1936 book, a claim later marked on a local Christmas tree farm.
New Egypt sits at the junction of Burlington, Monmouth, and Ocean counties, a unique tri‑county point that shapes its local identity.
